Plants

The living collection — plants grown, studied, and written up one at a time. Every plant gets a researched guide with its true name, its story, and exactly how to keep it thriving.

Ginkgo

Ginkgo biloba · Maidenhair Tree · Ginkgoaceae

The last living species of an order older than the dinosaurs, told through Blandy Experimental Farm’s famous Ginkgo Grove — 300+ seed-grown trees descended from one unnamed Charlottesville mother, a fifty-year experiment that answered its question after its asker died, a dying side being healed with bald cypress, and the embossed tags that keep every tree’s story. With a full teaching narration, a spoken note for every photograph, and the Pratt Ginkgo correction — the famous Rotunda tree is male, and never bore a seed.

Snow White Waffle Plant

Strobilanthes alternata ‘Snow White’ · Waffle Plant · Acanthaceae

A variegated waffle plant from the humid undergrowth of Java and Malaysia — crinkled, quilted leaves of light green splashed with white, edged in pink, over a vivid magenta-purple underside. It is a seedling of the purple ‘Exotica’ waffle plant, selected for its heavy white variegation. The full guide covers its identification, its botany, and the moist, steamy care it loves.

Aglaonema

Aglaonema spp. · Chinese Evergreen · Araceae

The low-light champion of the houseplant world, from rainforest floors in Southeast Asia where almost no direct sun ever lands. Broad leaves come painted in silver, cream, pink, and red across some two dozen species and hundreds of cultivars — and it has been kept for centuries as a good-luck plant. The full guide covers its care, its cold sensitivity, and one important caution: it is toxic to pets if chewed, so it lives up high, out of the cat’s reach.

Coral Cactus

Euphorbia lactea ‘Cristata’ · Crested Euphorbia · Euphorbiaceae

Not a cactus at all — a crested, variegated euphorbia whose growing point has fanned into a rippling coral of cream, sage, and blush pink, grafted onto a sturdy green stock to keep it strong. The full guide covers the graft that keeps it alive, the bright-shade, soak-and-dry care it wants, and one firm caution: its milky sap is toxic, so it lives up high, out of animals’ reach.

Hoya ‘Snow Caps’

Hoya lacunosa ‘Snow Caps’ · Silver-Splash Wax Vine · Apocynaceae

A small-leafed wax vine wearing a blizzard — every lance-shaped leaf splashed with silver, the brightest ones nearly white. The full guide shows how those lance leaves and wedge-shaped bases settle its identity against its heart-leafed cousin Hoya krohniana, the bright light that keeps it silver and brings on cinnamon-scented flowers, and the welcome news that it is non-toxic, safe around animals.

Read the Plant Guide

Aglaonema ‘Siam Aurora’

Aglaonema ‘Siam Aurora’ (red form) · Red Chinese Evergreen · Araceae

A Chinese evergreen poured in red-pink — lance leaves with a thin green rim and olive speckle still pushing through at the edges. The guide works the cultivar case honestly against its near kin ‘Red Anjamani’ and ‘Super Red’, lays out the bright light that keeps the red from fading back to green, the 59°F cold floor, and the ASPCA warning that keeps it out of animals’ reach.

Read the Plant Guide

Monstera adansonii

Monstera adansonii Schott · Swiss Cheese Vine · Araceae

A young Swiss cheese vine already wearing its windows — closed oval holes inside the blade, the trait that settles it against the split-leafed Rhaphidophora and the more-hole-than-leaf Monstera obliqua. The guide explains the pale chartreuse of youth and bright light, the lean toward the ‘Laniata’ form, LECA semi-hydro care with a one-third reservoir, and why a moss pole is this plant’s whole future. Toxic to cats — kept out of animals’ reach.
